The metasensor employed a deep CNN for direct width assessment 
from preprocessed crack images. It was trained and tested using a 
unique, large database of 19098 concrete crack width manual reference 
measurements and deployed to investigate the autogenous self-healing 
of 75-month-old high-strength concrete. The results of analogous in-
vestigations on concrete aged 2 and 20 months provided a background 
for evaluating the overall efficiency of self-healing for different com-
posite aging conditions. The differences between the self-healing of the 
75-month-old concrete on the externally exposed faces and internal 
parts of the composite are discussed. 
In addition to the aforementioned studies, the effects of the self- 
healing process and the microstructure of the composites were 
observed using optical and electron microscopy as well as X-ray 
computed tomography. 
The research plan and materials provided information on the possi-
bility of self-healing in mature high-strength concrete, the influence of 
aging processes, and the microstructural properties of composites on the 
effectiveness of these processes. 
This study considers samples prepared in laboratory or extracted 
from structural elements and self-healing investigated in laboratory 
conditions. The presented method has potential for in-situ self-healing 
monitoring, however, not demonstrated in the article. For in-situ self- 
healing monitoring the image capturing and preprocessing procedures 
need to be significantly modified. 
The proposed CNN models extract features from the image and apply 
them, rather than rely on arbitrary, analytic criteria such as threshold or 
gradient methods. Deep image analysis is performed directly from im-
ages and brightness profiles. This is a novel and effective approach to 
monitoring self-healing processes, as demonstrated in this article. The 
article also reports on the ability of mature high-strength concretes to 
self-heal at different depths relative to the outer surface, which has not 
been previously reported in the literature. 
Section 2 of the article presents the materials and samples used in the 
experiments. Section 3 includes the description of the employed 
research methods and procedures: image preprocessing, metasensor 
development, X-ray computed tomography scans, and optical and 
electron microscopy observations. In Section 4, the results of measure-

performed using a classification model. The input for this model is a 
photo with a crack, and the output is a binary image of this photo with 
crack area extraction. Subsequently, the crack width is determined. 
Herein, a different approach was used, a regression-based approach, in 
which the input was a crack photo, the intermediate product of image 
processing was a grid of profile lines, and the output was a measure of 
the crack width at each profile line. Classification of picture pixels into 
crack/non-crack categories was not performed explicitly. 
The CNN was implemented on a MATLAB programming platform 
using its Deep Learning toolbox [75]. The parameters defining the 
constructed network and learning algorithm were selected based on 
examples, guidelines [75], and multiple configuration trials. A CNN 
represents multiple levels of features obtained by consecutive nonlinear 
transformations, starting with raw input through subsequent additional 
abstract levels. Back-propagation is a mode for weight adjustment and 
model training in the implemented network. Specifically, stochastic 
gradient descent with a momentum optimizer is used for this purpose. 
The minibatch size was set as 128, initial learning rate was 10� 3, final 
learning rate was 10� 5, and number of epochs was 50. The implemented 
CNN consisted of 15 layers ordered as follows: image input, convolution, 
batch normalization, nonlinearity, pooling, convolution, batch normal-
ization, nonlinearity, pooling, convolution, batch normalization, 
nonlinearity, regularization, fully connected layer, and regression layer. 
The layer parameters are listed in Table 3. 
In common applications, the model accuracy is easily assessed 
because once the model is deployed, both the response and observed 
values can be determined, and thus, the model accuracy can be assessed. 
However, this was not the case in the targeted crack-width assessment 
problem. Reference observations necessary for evaluation are available 
only if manual reference measurements are performed. 
Deploying a machine learning model for new experimental data re-
quires that development and deployment datasets are consistent and 
that important features reflected in the data do not diverge. Therefore 
we recommend to control the data drift in the course of crack-width
